configuration.note: Ring closure, winding and CRS84 bounds are checked when the file is read. What is NOT checkable here is whether the lines are where the author meant them to be: a traced territory is a reading of a printed wash, and experiment 145 records that as not established.

ports.note: No input ports: it reads a file. Emits the existing `polygons` port type and needed no new one, which is why the seven widgets that already consume polygons -- clip, summarize, stack, fill gaps, and the map and chart and table outputs -- accept it without change. That reuse is the whole value of the widget; a new port type would have reached none of them.

ontology.note: No mapping to an external vocabulary yet. The receipt states the file, its digest, the feature count, the property each feature was named by, and that nothing was clipped, simplified or reprojected.

changes.description: Reads a published polygon layer from a GeoJSON file and emits it as the existing `polygons` value, so everything that already consumes polygons accepts it. Until this existed, seven node types emitted polygons and every one DERIVED them from something else -- points allocated to cells, a table joined to an area, a hull, a corridor, a stack of other layers -- so a layer that existed as a file had no way into a workflow at all. South London's `geo/map2-water-supply-zones.geojson` had been in that repository since 2026-10-24 and had reached a workflow never: the three territories Snow drew, of which the purple one, the area where the pipes of both companies are intermingled, is the zone where attributing supply by sub-district misclassifies. READ AS PUBLISHED is the distinction it enforces: nothing is clipped, simplified or reprojected, and a file whose coordinates are not CRS84 degrees is refused rather than converted, because converting it silently would hand on a different shape from the one its author published. The feature-naming property is chosen by the practitioner and never inferred from a column name. Admitted under the review in experiment 145, where D2 turns on the distinction between a study area -- the frame, one boundary -- and a layer, which is many attributed features; the practitioner settled it by revising the study area to the enclosing extent so the sub-districts and the river become layers within it.

evidence.note: Unit tested against the three MultiPolygon territories the South London repository ships, which is the layer the widget was built for: 153, 128 and 107 vertices across six rings, every vertex preserved, the attributes carried as published, and the three supply categories read from the property the practitioner named. The HOLES are asserted explicitly, because they are what makes reading as published worth enforcing: Lambeth's territory is one part of three rings -- an outer boundary of 107 positions and two interior rings of 9 and 12 -- so there are enclaves inside the Lambeth zone that Lambeth did not supply, which no count of features reveals and which a simplifier would take first. Refusals covered: coordinates outside CRS84 bounds (easting and northing in metres, which is what an export from a projected CRS gives), a geometry that is not a polygon, an unclosed ring, a named property no feature carries, a file that is not a FeatureCollection, an empty one, and one larger than a study's own geometry. What this does not establish is whether the traced lines are where Snow's printed wash actually was: the geometry is a reading of a colour boundary on a scanned plate, and experiment 145 records it as a reading rather than a measurement.
